newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo central bank to stick to tight money policy.
newsitem.headline: Yugo central bank to stick to tight money policy.

text.p: The Yugoslav central bank (NBY) will stick to its tight monetary policy to maintain the stability of the dinar and the economy, according to a leading central bank official.

"There is no reason to be suspicious about the stability of the dinar," the bank's deputy governor Ratko Banovic told Reuters at the weekend following a symposium of 400 leading Yugoslav financial and economic experts at this Montenegran seaside resort.
The official also rejected calls by exporting companies to devalue the dinar, now pegged at 3.3 to the German mark.

Banovic denied that the central bank was under increasing pressure from the governments of rump Yugoslavia and of its two constituent republics, Serbia and Montenegro, to print new money to finance the cash-starved economy and losses.
"On the contrary, the federal and both republic governments are appealing for tight control of monetary policy."
He admitted however that pressure on the bank to print new money was coming from commercial banks and industry.
"They are used to asking the central bank for help whenever they have (financial) problems," he said.

In 1993 the presses worked around the clock to print new money in a desperate bid to combat international sanctions imposed on Yugoslavia for its role in the Bosnian war, driving inflation to dizzying levels of 60 percent a day.

Banovic said the NBY would regulate the volume of money supply and stability of currencies and prices using available mechanisms, adding: "But we will not help the financial recovery of the banks by just printing money."

The central bank's foreign currency reserves, he said, had risen by 40 million German marks since December. It had sold half a million marks to Yugoslav companies to finance imports since December 1, but had bought 540 million marks over the same period, he added.
The bank does not publish regular figures on foreign currency reserves, but in mid-May they stood at $335 million.
The bank was closely monitoring the rise in money supply (M1) in order to control it at the level which would preserve currency and price stability, he said.
He recalled that the NBY had introduced new measures in August to maintain and slow down the rising tendency of M1 and to force banks to resolve their insolvency problem by themselves.
"We just want them to do their own job," he said. "They should not expect us to do something that is not our job. We believe the new measures will help currency and price stability."
Banovic suggested that banks and companies short of working capital should raise it by liquidating assets such as real estate, stocks and foreign currency.
"They must re-establish contacts with their partners abroad and try to get credits to maintain their solvency," he added.
Banovic said the NBY had rejected demands by some sectors of the Yugoslav economy currently suffering big losses for the bank to finance their production.
"It could ease the situation and increase production but only in the short term," he said, adding that any gains would soon be neutralised by price increases and inflation.
Annual inflation in August was running at 99.2 percent.
Banovic also rejected calls for changes in the dinar exchange rate by export firms who argued that the currency was overvalued.

He said that according to NBY's analysis of price increases here and abroad since Belgrade introduced a drastic monetary reform in February 1994, the dinar was now undervalued by two or three percent.
"There is still some room left for the prices to rise and there is no reason to even contemplate changing the currenct exchange rate," Banovic said.

The dinar was devalued by 70 percent in November, bringing it into line with the black market rate of 3.3 dinars to one German mark, when it real value was 2.5 dinars to the mark. The current black market rate is 3.4 dinars to the mark.
